#7857. The Best Propane Heaters of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

By Glenda Taylor, Additional research provided by Timothy Dale, Bob Beacham

Published Nov 5, 2026 9:00 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Propane heaters are an incredibly effective way to quickly heat a medium to large living space using liquid propane (LP) as fuel, making them suitable for a range of heating needs.

We researched more than 30 propane heaters and then selected several top-rated models for hands-on testing by the Bob Vila test team. We also consulted Alex Rushwin, technical service manager for Enerco Group, manufacturer of the ever-popular Mr. Heater line of propane heaters.

Today’s propane heaters burn cleaner and are safer than early models. “Mr. Heater patented the first indoor propane heater back in 2000,” Rushwin says, “and that was a huge step forward for portable propane heat.” Since then, Mr. Heater has improved on the technology, and their indoor heaters are safer than ever.

Finding the best propane heater for your purposes depends on how you will use it, where it will be used, the heat output you need, and the important safety features included. Our favorite of the bunch was Mr. Heater’s MH9BX model for its portable design and quick heating capabilities. While intended use varies, each of the following models excelled in our hands-on tests and earned its spot in this lineup of the best propane heaters.

Bottom line: Propane heaters are versatile and efficient, with models suited for various spaces and needs. Safety and portability are essential considerations.

The following are some of the best propane heaters on the market in their respective categories. They were selected for quality and price, with a focus on the shopping considerations mentioned above.

Rushwin says that Mr. Heater’s Buddy series is one of its most popular sellers, and it’s been one of our favorites for years, as it was our standby heater for mountain camping adventures. The MH9BX was new to us though, and we were impressed right off the bat by the new swivel-connector feature that allowed us to twist the 1-pound propane bottle into position with ease. Some of the older models didn’t have the swivel connector, so good going, Mr. Heater! That’s a huge plus.

The Buddy MH9BX has an attractive design with a sturdy fold-down carrying handle that makes it easy to pick up and take wherever it’s needed. The heater has a choice of two heat outputs, either 4,000 or 9,000 BTUs, making it capable of heating up to 225 square feet of space. We tested the MH9BX in a 180-square foot room, and on high, it raised the temperature from 70 to 78 degrees Fahrenheit in just 30 minutes. It’s a radiant heater, so it warms objects, not the air, but the heated objects in turn warmed up the room.

This heater is able to burn propane at near-100 percent efficiency, which makes it an option for indoor applications. Its oxygen-depletion sensor (ODS) ensures that the oxygen level never drops to a dangerous point. Plus, its tip-over safety mechanism immediately shut the heater off when we tipped it over.

Read our full review: Mr. Heater MH9BX Portable Buddy Heater

Get the Mr. Heater MH9BX propane heater at Amazon, The Home Depot, or Walmart.

Our second Mr. Heater pick is the Little Buddy MH4B, which provides instant warmth at an attractive price point. Not only is the Little Buddy easy on the wallet, but it’s also simple to carry along when tailgating or just spending a little time bird-watching on a chilly day. It’s an excellent pick for supplemental indoor emergency heat, too. It burns clean and comes with a low-oxygen sensor that shuts it off if the oxygen level in the space drops to an unhealthy level.

The Little Buddy is designed to heat spaces up to 95 square feet, so we tested it in a bathroom, where it raised the room’s temperature by 15 degrees Fahrenheit in 30 minutes. Keep in mind that temperature increases will vary depending on the type of space, starting temperature, and whether the space is insulated or if it is being used as a tent heater without any insulation.

Like its big brother, the Buddy heater, Little Buddy is a radiant propane heater, and it warms nearby objects—and people. We found it excellent for warming our gloved hands outdoors, but it doesn’t blow hot air. The tip-over shutoff turned the heater off immediately when we laid the Little Buddy on its side.

While this little propane heater isn’t powerful enough for warming up large rooms, it’s an excellent small heater that’s safe for indoor use.

Get the Mr. Heater Little Buddy propane heater at Walmart.

Tank tops aren’t just sleeveless attire for hot summer days. The Camplux Tank Top propane heater attaches to the top of a 20-pound or larger propane tank, and it quickly warms nearby objects or people—making it a handy heater for outdoor use or in ventilated shops and garages.

This is not an in-home model; the manufacturer suggests having a 0.5-square-foot opening for fresh air for every 15,000 BTUs being used. For example, if using both burners simultaneously on the highest setting (total of 30,000 BTUs), opening a 24-inch wide window just 1 inch would be sufficient. A door does not need to be wide open; just crack a window.

It comes with two radiant burners and attaches securely to the steel collar at the top of a standard propane tank. It was easy to connect to the tank and held firmly throughout our tests. We tested the Camplux dual-burner propane heater in a mobile workshop with an open-end wall.

It was simple to connect to the top of the propane tank and easy to light—but be aware this is a manual-light heater; we had to insert a lit match in a hole in the side of the reflective cover and then slowly turn on the propane. It fired right up. Each side lights and operates independently.

The Camplux Tank Top heater provided a lot of radiant heat—so much that we couldn’t stand any closer than about 4 feet without feeling uncomfortably hot when running it on the high setting. On the low setting, it was more tolerable, but it still puts out a lot of heat. It didn’t appreciably raise the temperature in the mobile shop, but that was due to one end of the shop trailer being completely open, which allowed cool breezes to blow through.

This is a powerful, no-frills propane heater for use in a ventilated workshop or on a jobsite.

Get the Camplux propane heater at Amazon.

The East Oak patio heater offers ambience and is a stunning focal point for a chilly outdoor winter gathering, but plan on spending at least an hour or more assembling all the parts. As we were setting it up, more than once we wondered whether the heater would be worth the hassle of trying to peel off the stubborn protective blue film—with some pieces coming off in tiny bits rather than sheets—and then putting together literally everything on the unit.

Once we got the East Oak pyramid heater together and fired up, we changed our minds—it was worth it. The glass cylinder in the pyramid’s center showcases beautiful dancing flames that rise to the upper vent, where the heat is reflected downward and outward toward anyone standing nearby. The outdoor temperature and breezes will affect its heating range, but we could feel warmth when standing about 10 feet away.

This is strictly an outdoor propane heater, so don’t take it in the house—it needs ample ventilation. It comes with tip-over shut-off protection and also shuts down propane flow if the flame goes out to keep propane gas from leaking into the air. We tested both, and they worked well. It connects to a 20-pound propane tank that fits right inside its base.

The East Oak pyramid heater also provides a good amount of light, so it can be used as supplemental lighting for outdoor entertaining. We really liked this tower heater, but we would have been happier with our experience if it had come at least partially assembled. It’s a lot to put together for even those familiar with assembling tools and appliances.

Get the East Oak propane heater at Walmart.

For many DIYers, the garage is the only covered space available for working on projects. Losing that space to cold weather is avoidable when using a propane heater like this one from Mr. Heater, which can heat a space of up to 450 square feet. The heater has three radiant-heat output settings, including a low setting of 6,000 BTUs; a medium setting of 12,000 BTUs; and a high setting that reaches 18,000 BTUs.

We put the MH18CH in a corner in a three-stall garage for testing. It was a chilly day, and also cold the day before testing, so the temperature in the garage was 53 degrees Fahrenheit. We turned the MH18CH on the high setting, and within 30 minutes, the temperature in the nearest stall rose to 61 degrees Fahrenheit, but the farthest stall registered just 54 degrees Fahrenheit. This was in an uninsulated garage, and results would vary in different-size garages or an insulated garage.

The propane heater has a space in the back designed to accommodate a 20-pound propane tank so that users can move the entire unit around easily on the four attached swivel wheels. This product also has a tip-over safety mechanism and an ODS sensor to automatically shut down the heater if the oxygen level gets too low.

This is a nice portable little propane heater that can be rolled around a garage or shop, which is a convenient way to heat the space where work is being done.

Get the Mr. Heater MH18CH propane heater at Lowe’s, Ace Hardware, or The Home Depot.

We examined several factors when choosing the propane heaters we wanted to test. Safety was essential, and beyond that, we looked at heat output (British thermal units, or BTUs), heater type (convection vs. radiant), ease of use, and cost. We considered the brand; after all, Mr. Heater and Dyna-Glo are well-respected names in the propane heater world. Still, we didn’t automatically dismiss smaller niche brands if the heaters were durable, safe, and highly rated.

The actual testing of the heaters was pretty simple; after all, they serve one primary purpose: to warm up a space or warm up nearby objects and people. We noted how easy (or challenging) the heaters were to assemble, and then we connected them to propane tanks or bottles, as called for by the manufacturer.

We tested the heaters’ ignition features and noted how much heat they produced and how quickly. Each propane heater was scored using a rubric. The better the heater performed on a test, the more points we awarded. After testing, we averaged the points to determine our top pick and to establish the best uses for each model.

Before choosing the best propane heater for a patio, garage, or home, take a look below to learn about some of the most important shopping considerations that can help you select a heater that suits your needs.

Propane heaters must have the pilot light ignited before the unit will produce any heat. Keep in mind that igniting the pilot light requires the gas to be turned on. These units typically have one of three different ignition methods: manual ignition, push-button ignition, and continuous ignition.

One of the main benefits of having a propane heater is that they are usually portable and can be connected to a small or large propane tank. It’s relatively easy to take a portable propane heater to another room, to the garage, or to the outdoors. However, if the heater will be used in one or two main locations, the product needs to be suited to those main areas.

In general, only heaters that accommodate 1-pound propane bottles are suitable for use indoors. Those that connect to 20-pound or larger propane tanks should be connected to a hose that’s long enough to locate the tank outdoors. The exception is models designed to hold 20-pound tanks that can be used in ventilated garages or workshops. Read the manufacturer’s safety precautions carefully.

The best outdoor propane heaters have enough heating power to deal with the rapid dissipation of heat that will naturally occur in a wide-open space. For those who want a great camping heater, a large outdoor option might be best. An alternative is a handheld propane heater that will keep people warm instead of heating the entire area. Some users may prefer to have a wall-mounted propane heater to save floor space and to keep the heater out of reach from kids and pets.

Portability is one of the features that sets propane heaters apart from electric or natural gas heaters, but not all propane heaters can really make the claim that they are portable. Some propane heaters that have built-in fans or other electronic components will typically need to be plugged into a power source, despite their main fuel being propane.

If portability is a key personal factor, then a propane heater that doesn’t need an electrical power source is often a better choice. A smaller size and a carrying handle will make it easier to pick up and move around. However, if a larger heater is needed for commercial or industrial applications, there are powerful propane heaters that sit on a set of wheels. The wheels make it easier to move the heater around a space.

Whenever using any type of heating device, it’s critical to be certain that all the necessary precautions are being followed to ensure that no one is at risk. This includes the proper storage of propane tanks and adequate ventilation when the heater is in use. There are other safety features to consider like overheating protection, a tip-over mechanism, and an oxygen-depletion sensor.

The heat output of a propane heater is normally measured in BTUs, with each BTU equal to the heat it would take to increase the temperature of 1 pound of water by 1 degree Fahrenheit. The BTU rating of a propane heater can range widely from as low as 3,000 BTUs to higher than 300,000 BTUs. The best BTU output for a heater will depend on how and where it will be used. For example, outdoor heaters naturally require a higher heat output.

Before deciding on a product, measure the room that needs to be heated. To help figure out which heater is best suited to a particular need, most manufacturers list the BTU output and include the approximate square footage that is appropriate for the heater. For example, a heater with a maximum of 10,000 BTUs may heat a space of approximately 250 square feet, while a unit that has a maximum of 18,000 BTUs will have no problem with 450 square feet.

Size is a factor that can impact where the heater will be used, how it is set up, and whether it’s a portable heater or a stationary unit. A small heater can often be picked up and carried around without a problem. Always check with the manufacturer, but smaller units usually can be used both indoors and outdoors without producing harmful fumes, as these smaller heaters tend to burn fuel at a slower pace.

Large propane heaters can take up a lot of space, which can become a safety hazard if they are too close to flammable objects in the room. Their size also may affect the placement in the room, or it may limit the product to outdoor use. However, a larger propane heater is able to hold an equally large propane tank so it won’t need to be replaced as frequently as the fuel in a small heater.

There are many advantages to owning a propane heater. One of the defining features is that these heaters are typically fueled by a portable container of propane, giving users the freedom to carry them from room to room or even take them out into the middle of the woods when camping. Unless the heater has a built-in fan unit, users won’t have to be tethered to a power outlet with this heater.

There is also the benefit of cost savings with a propane heater. This is because the average cost of electricity is higher than the average cost of propane. With a propane heater, there is a wide range of heat-output options that can increase well beyond the capabilities of an electric or natural gas heater, allowing users to rapidly heat up large outdoor spaces.

Whether you want to supplement heat for a greenhouse or have access to a source of emergency heat when the power goes out, propane could be the answer. If you still have questions about propane heaters, read below to find the answers to some of the most commonly asked questions.

While it’s unlikely, if the propane heater is not designed for indoor use, it could put off some carbon monoxide fumes. If you are using the heater in a larger enclosed space like a garage, make sure that you have a carbon monoxide detector installed to warn you of any danger.

It is generally considered to be a bad idea to have a lit propane heater in your bedroom because it will quickly burn up the oxygen in an enclosed room, which could cause the oxygen levels to drop. Fortunately many of today’s indoor propane heaters, such as those made by Mr. Heater, come with low-oxygen sensors that shut the unit off if the oxygen level in the room drops.

Outdoor propane heaters need proper ventilation to ensure that you don’t get carbon monoxide poisoning. Indoor propane heaters—often called “vent-free” heaters—do not put off carbon monoxide, but ventilation is still necessary to ensure healthy oxygen levels in the room.

While it’s essential to always follow the manufacturer’s directions for safe use, here are the basic steps for how to light a propane heater:1. Turn on the propane tank.2. Adjust the knob on the front or side of the heater to the “start” or “light” position.3. Push the knob in and hold it to send gas to the unit. Continue holding the knob in for 30 seconds to ensure adequate gas flow.4. Press the igniter button firmly until you hear a click. You may need to press it more than once on some heaters.5. Adjust the control knob to the desired temperature.

#7856. "The Time, the Opportunity, and the Need to Reclaim the Republican Party from Trump and Trumpism"

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

I thought I'd pass along this smart and readable analysis from Bill Otis (Ringside at the Reckoning); as I've mentioned before, he and his coauthor Paul Mirengoff are my go-to people for hardheaded, pragmatic, but principled conservative views. They are probably on balance more conservative than I am, but I always much enjoy their legal and political commentary. An excerpt:

In an election where overwhelmingly the preeminent issue was affordability — in other and more candid words, the increasingly obvious decline in the standard of living huge numbers of people are feeling — what has Trump been occupying himself with? Here's a partial list: Building the White House ballroom (from which, in a tone deaf rendition that defies description) he gave his election post-mortem; re-doing the East Potomac Golf Course to make it a "premium" experience; building a Triumphal Arch no one asked for or thought about when they elected him; demanding prosecutions for imaginary vandalism at the Reflecting Pool; invading Greenland; making Canada the 51st state; re-naming Lake Ontario; re-naming the Gulf of Mexico; and perhaps most prominently, making sure his name gets put on the Kennedy Center even though he had nothing to do with its creation. Then there are numerous other items: Trump passports, Trump one-dollar gold coins, and "commemorative" $100 bills, to name three.

Exactly what does this Adventure in Narcissism seem like to the voter — actually, the millions of voters — who feel like they're being stretched thin? You don't need a florid imagination to answer that one. They gave their answer last night.

It's not like Trump has had no successes. He's made three excellent Supreme Court appointments. He has tackled corrosive and unjust racial preferences like no one else had the guts to. He declines to bow to transgender bullying. Objective economic data show that, whatever "feelings" may be, the economy grew at a healthy clip just this last quarter. He used force with Iran when, for nearly 50 years before him, Presidents were content to kick the can down the road as the mullahs got closer and closer to getting the atomic bomb.

These are considerable and important achievements, not less so because Trump often acts like an oaf. But his character flaws throw a wrench into nearly everything he does. It's less that he's an oaf than that he's a child, far too often content to do what's quick and easy while leaving to adults what's messy and hard. The catch is: He's supposed to be the adult. The main thing behind the failures that got Trump his butt-kicking last night is not his classlessness, his carefree attitude [toward] the truth or his gargantuan self-absorption.

The whole thing, as usual, is much worth reading.

#7854. The Best Roof Cleaners of 2026, Tested

By Mike Larson, Additional research provided by Tom Scalisi

Published Nov 5, 2026 9:30 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

While many homeowners concentrate on maintaining the ground-level features of their homes, a roof cleaner can help keep the roof looking its best. Often, not until black streaks and patches of moss show up do homeowners realize their roof needs some attention. However, with a good roof washing, even the dirtiest roof can be restored.

While hiring one of the best roof cleaning services is always an option, a roof wash can be a pretty simple DIY job for roofs that are easily accessed. To clean your roof, all you need to do is block out some time, arm yourself with one of the best roof cleaners, and get to work. We evaluated several of the best roof cleaners and even hands-on tested them to provide a list of the products best suited to cut through the dirt, grime, and sludge, revealing your roof’s true colors. After testing, we chose the 30 Seconds Ready-to-Use Outdoor Cleaner as our top pick. We liked it for its versatility, large coverage area, and ease of use.

The cleaners on our list are widely available to order online, so you can have your pick delivered right to your door to save on professional roof cleaning costs. Read on to find out what to look for when shopping so you can choose the best roof cleaners for your needs.

Bottom line: The 30 Seconds Outdoor Cleaner stands out as the best roof cleaner of 2026, offering an effective and user-friendly solution for DIY enthusiasts.

Our Ratings: Ease of Application 5/5; Effectiveness 4/5; Portability 5/5; Ease of Cleanup 5/5; Value 4/5

For a roof wash that really does the job, 30 Seconds Outdoor Cleaner proved to be the best roof cleaner for a variety of reasons. Effective and easy to apply, this product stood out among our group of tested products.

To start with, it actually does live up to its name. Since there’s no mixing of dilution required, all a user has to do is spray it on the surface they want to clean (we tested it on concrete, brick, shingles, and metal roofing), wait 30 seconds (although we found a full minute is even more effective), and then spray it off with a hose. No power-washing is required.

This roof treatment product is also easy to move around with. When you’re climbing on a roof with even a slight pitch, safety is paramount, so it’s important to have a handled container that’s easy to move around with.

The bleach smell is the only thing we didn’t care for with this product; it’s more than faint, but not overpowering. However, wearing a mask or some nose plugs is a small price to pay to get the full effectiveness of 30 Seconds Outdoor Cleaner.

What our tester says: “This was hands-down the most effective cleaner we tested, and wearing a mask for the bleach smell is a small trade-off for how well it works.”—Mike Larson, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the 30 Seconds roof cleaner at Amazon (2-pack) or Do it Best.

There are multiple factors to consider when shopping for an appropriate roof cleaner, from the surface of the roof itself to the specific dirt issues that homeowners are faced with. Our list of recommended products covers the wide array of cleaners available for mold, moss, and mildew to provide the best suggestions for each scenario.

To choose which products to test, we scoured the web for customer reviews, researched all products being considered, and looked for products that we felt could stand up to the rigorous testing we had planned. Since heavy-duty solutions often use bleach and other harsh chemicals, which are not always what shoppers are looking for, we made sure to also include a product that’s more environmentally friendly.

Our testing process included a start-to-finish cleaning session with each product. We applied the roof cleaner by following the instructions on each product, then followed the instructions for cleaning. A typical test had us spraying the product on the affected area of roof, allowing it to sit for an amount of time defined on the product’s instructions (sometimes doing a little scrubbing), and then rinsing the product away.

This section will outline the most important considerations to keep in mind while you’re shopping for the best roof cleaner for your home. It covers aspects including the different types of roofing materials, how much coverage you’ll get, and how easy the products are to use.

Don’t rush out and set up the ladder quite yet. You first need to educate yourself on the different types of roof cleaners available. They all work a little differently, and some are much harsher on the environment than others. It’s important to do a little research before you choose the best roof cleaner for your needs.

For particularly stubborn stains and discolorations, beach-based cleaners might be the way to go. They’re so strong, in fact, that you don’t even need to scrub or rinse down the roof for them to work. Simply apply them to the roof and let them dry. The bleach will eat through the dirt and grime all on its own.

The thing about bleach-based chemicals, though, is that they’re extremely harsh. Breathing in their vapors can cause coughing, lung irritation, and shortness of breath. Any overspray (or runoff when it rains) can wreak havoc on your plants. These cleaners are so strong, in fact, that it’s best to keep your windows closed for a few days to avoid the fumes and odors.

Bleach isn’t the only chemical manufacturers use to restore a roof to its former glory. Some formulas feature ammonia, copper sulfate, and trisodium phosphate, all of which can do a great job of removing the stains, molds, and mosses that grow on roofs.

These formulas can be harsh on your plants as well, though usually to a lesser degree than bleach-based cleaners. They rarely require the user to scrub or apply a second application, and in most cases, there’s no need to keep your windows closed after application. Since they usually come in concentrates, they typically need to be mixed with water unless you have a really stubborn stain.

If you’re looking for a safer, less environmentally detrimental approach to cleaning your roof, check out an eco-friendly cleaner. These formulas break up the dirt, algae, and mold on your roof without the inherent dangers of chemical and bleach compounds.

Eco-friendly cleaners are safe for your kids, plants, and the wildlife that might roam through your property. While it’s entirely possible to have some type of allergic reaction to these products, they’re generally safe to use and less irritating.

Since eco-friendly cleaners tend to use oxygen to break down dirt and roof-loving molds and algae, they work best with a bit of agitation. You’ll likely have to scrub most of your stains and discolorations away, so having a long-handled brush will be incredibly helpful.

If you want to blast your roof clean, you can always set up a pressure washer and get to work. The pump inside your pressure washer boosts the amount of pressure with which the water comes out of the nozzle, knocking dirt and film clear off your roof shingles.

But pressure washers can also blast your roof shingles right off, so take care when you’re doing any kind of roof pressure washing.

To help increase your pressure washer’s effectiveness, there are many products available that can be mixed into the water. If you don’t use a chemical, though, be aware that water alone might not kill any residual moss and algae.

Raw chlorine, also known as sodium hydrochlorite, cleans a roof while also killing mold and mildew spores. This compound is made to sanitize, removing bacteria at the same time it cleans up stains and grime. When diluting, it’s important to ensure that raw chlorine solutions never comprise more than 30 percent of the roof cleaning solution, and it’s important that they’re thoroughly rinsed off after use.

The first thing you’ll want to consider are all the materials that make up your roof to ensure you use the right product.

Less-durable materials like vinyl and rubber membranes found on flat roofs or RVs are particularly susceptible to damage from harsh chemicals. Heavy-duty cleaners can wear down the roofing components faster than if you used an eco-friendly option.

Tougher materials, like asphalt, metal, or slate roofs, can take much stronger chemicals. You’ll be able to use bleach or chemical-based cleaners without worrying about what they’ll do to your roof’s finish.

The best roof cleaners can be broken down into two options: eco-friendly and chemical. Eco-friendly options don’t contain harmful chemicals, so they’re safe to use on roofs above gardens and plants. The composition of chemical-based products, on the other hand, isn’t always so environmentally conscious.

Chemical-based cleaners often use chemicals such as ammonia, copper sulfate, and trisodium phosphate. They can be harsh, but they’re extremely effective at removing the stains as well as the molds, algae, and mosses that cause them. Simply diluting them to the manufacturer’s recommended mixture does reduce some of the risk, so it’s important to read and follow the directions carefully.

Not all roof cleaners can cover the same amount of square footage, so it’s important to understand how much roof a bottle or jug can handle. To do this, you have to know the size of your roof first: Simply multiply each section of your roof’s width by its height. Tally each of those sections. The number you get after you add up all the different planes is your square footage.

Some of the best roof cleaners come in concentrated formulas that you can dilute for maximum coverage. While their bottles might be small, they can often cover thousands of square feet of roof if you dilute them correctly.

Cleaning your roof isn’t all that much fun, so the process should be made as painless as possible. Finding a user-friendly product can make all the difference.

A chemical that you can spray on your roof and leave to do its work is by far the easiest way to clean your roof. Other chemicals might require you to scrub the surface, which can be a challenge if you have a high roof.

Also, consider the application. Although spray bottles are easy to use, covering a large area with a spray bottle is difficult, so they’re ideal for smaller roofs. Concentrate bottles that attach to the end of your hose make applying the chemical to larger roofs extremely easy, but you might not be able to reach high peaks from the ground. Whatever product you choose, be sure to select one that you can apply easily to your particular roof.

Ultimately, how well the product works at removing stains, molds, algae, and discolorations is one of the most important factors to keep in mind. The more effective the product, the fewer coats you’ll have to apply, and the less often you’ll have to apply it.

Less-effective products don’t always kill the root cause of the discoloration, even if the stain disappears. If that root is still present, there’s a good chance that whatever caused the stain will come back. This means you’ll have to apply your product more often to keep up with it.

Harsh chemicals are by far the most effective way to get rid of stains and often require just one application. However, using eco-friendly products might require you to commit to more frequent cleanings or follow-up applications.

For those who have additional questions about choosing or using the best roof cleaner, this section contains answers to some of the most frequently asked questions.

Many of the best roof cleaner manufacturers recommend cleaning your roof every 12 to 24 months to ensure your roof stays clean and free from growths. But whenever you notice discoloration, moss, mold, or mildew, it’s a good idea to give your roof a spray.

It depends on the cleaner. Many of the heaviest-duty cleaners will damage vinyl or fabric awnings, while some biodegradable or lighter-duty cleaners will work quite well. However, it’s important to always refer to the product label before use.

Most roof cleaners are available in concentrated forms, and you can mix them to whatever strength you’d like. If you’re planning to use yours at full strength, it’s a good idea to test it on a smaller space first to see how it affects your surface.

There are a few steps you can take to minimize your roof cleaner’s impact on your plants.1. Cover your plants in tarps or plastic sheeting.2. Use only as much chemical as necessary.3. Ensure your gutters aren’t clogged so any chemical-laden rainwater can flow away from the eaves.4. Water your plants heavily before, during, and after using your cleaner. Diluting the concentration of chemicals is the best way to lessen the risk of damage.

Basic safety items like goggles, a respirator, and gloves are certainly important. You can also wear long sleeves. Using a long-handled brush or roller, or a garden sprayer, can make applying your roof cleaner easier.

#7851. 5 Annual Flowers I Bring Indoors to Brighten Winter

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 5, 2026 10:34 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

I like to grow exotic species indoors for flowering during the winter months, either under grow lights or on a sunny windowsill. However, I also save a few annuals from my garden, usually container types that don’t require large amounts of light to flourish. After all, annuals are easy to bring into flowering, while some tropicals and other perennials can be challenging to coax into bloom.

Plants like geraniums (Pelargonium spp.) and flowering maples (Abutilon spp.) can be long-blooming indoor annual flowers. In addition, the annuals listed below can often bloom longer indoors, extending the life of your annual flowers and brightening rooms in winter.

Although I bring tuberous begonias indoors over winter, I always let them die back to their tubers, since they require a period of dormancy to bloom well the following summer. However, I’ve found that other begonia species such as the wax begonia (B. semperflorens) will flower cheerfully almost year-round. After all, its species name means “ever-blooming.”

I’ve learned to be careful not to overwater the plants during winter as I have had favorites, including the double-flowered cultivar pictured above, succumb to root rot. But otherwise, wax begonias are easy-care plants that can add indoor winter color.

Common impatiens (Impatiens walleriana) plants flower busily both outdoors and indoors. Because they root easily in water, I often take cuttings of them in late summer to pot up later, but sometimes just prune back a mature plant to bring inside.

The semidouble type of Busy Lizzy is seldom available in my area, so I saved one of my I. walleriana ‘Athena’ plants last autumn, and it continued to perform under the lights over winter and in the container pictured in the banner image this summer. I’ve occasionally also grown more unusual cultivars of impatiens under lights, including Giant Balsam (I. grandis, pictured above) and rare species such as Blue Diamond Impatiens (I. namchabarwensis).

Coleus cuttings also root quickly in water. That’s a good thing because the Big Bad Boys cultivar I grew this summer lived up to its name by eventually growing to 2 feet, even when packed into a container with other shade-loving annuals. So, I will need to take cuttings or prune the plant to restore it to a suitable size for grow lights.

Since coleus annuals, such as the blazingly red type above, are grown for their boldly colored foliage rather than their nondescript blooms, I usually try to pinch out any bud stalks that sprout. Otherwise, these are easy-care indoor annual flowers.

Due to their preference for cool and somewhat humid conditions, fuchsias often do well under my basement grow lights. And, yes, their cuttings, too, will root easily in water should you not want to bring an entire hanging basket indoors.

As with most annuals, fuchsias won’t bloom as heavily in the house as they do outside, but they will make some flowers. I believe those pictured—blooming under lights one late December—are the elegantly elongated Bolivian fuchsia (F. boliviana). But the typical hanging basket type called Lady’s Eardrops (F. magellanica) also will perform as indoor winter plants under the right conditions.

I have a very old Lantana camara plant with a large, gnarled and knotted trunk that looks more like a bonsai specimen than a potted annual. But it proves that lantanas, also called shrub verbenas, can last almost indefinitely if protected during winter. In fact, they can be perennial plants in warm growing zones.(7 to 11).

However, I’ve found that my plant will drop most of its leaves after being brought indoors. It isn’t dying, just adapting to new light levels. It might qualify as one of the fragrant indoor plants since its leaves have a peculiar odor that some people compare to citrus and others to gasoline.

Because my windows are drafty and don’t receive much illumination during winter, I place most of my flowering indoor plants under grow lights, either fluorescent or LED. (I am gradually switching over to the latter, since they make more light while using less energy.)

I use 4-foot fixtures and keep most of the plants in the basement, where conditions are cooler and more humid than in the rest of the house. Since some of my plants require short days to bloom, I keep the lights on timers so they are on for no more than 12 hours per day.

These full-spectrum grow light panels are lightweight and low-heat, making them our top pick for boosting indoor plants during winter.

One problem with having tropical plants and other flowering annuals in the basement is that out of sight often means out of mind. So, I have to remember to trudge down the stairs with a watering can at least once per day. Since it is easy to accidentally overwater plants in winter, I test the surface of their soil with a fingertip first and only water when that surface is dry.

If a plant is blooming, I often bring it upstairs to enjoy before returning it to its original position under the lights. That is my way of feeding my flower addiction during winter.

All You Need to Care for Your Lawn & Garden

Keeping your grass green and your plants thriving doesn’t just take a green thumb—it starts with the right tools and supplies.

#7849. Why You Should Pay Attention to Diamond-Shaped Signs on Trucks

Those metal diamonds on the back of trucks serve a purpose. Learn how hazmat placard holders work and what an empty one actually means.

Drivers have a lot to pay attention to on the road. They watch their speed, check their mirrors, and keep an eye out for sudden stops. But one detail most drivers probably haven’t given much thought to is the diamond-shaped designs on the back of trucks, even after seeing them countless times.

No, they aren’t decorations. It’s a small detail that serves an important safety purpose, especially if there’s an accident involving dangerous cargo. Learn how the holders work, what the warning signs mean, and why some appear empty.

They’re called hazmat placard holders. These metal frames hold warning signs that identify certain hazardous materials a truck might be carrying. The bare diamond in the photo is simply a holder. Its lines and clips don’t send any special message to other drivers.

Truck operators leave the holders attached and change the signs depending on their cargo. Some hold removable placards, while others have several signs that drivers can flip between. Labelmaster, a company that makes flip-placard systems, explains that drivers can change the warning without replacing the holder.

The placards use colors, words, and symbols to identify different hazards. Red often indicates flammable materials, while a black-and-white sign marked “CORROSIVE” warns about chemicals that can cause damage. Other signs identify dangerous gases, explosives, or toxic substances.

“Placards serve as an easily identifiable, visual source of information used by millions of workers in the transportation, public safety, and hazmat industries,” according to the U.S. Department of Transportation’s Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA).

These warnings help emergency responders recognize potential hazards during an accident or spill. Some placards also display numbers that identify specific hazardous materials.

An empty holder may mean the truck doesn’t need to display a warning for its current shipment. Trucking companies leave the frames attached because their vehicles might carry different types of cargo from one trip to the next. An empty holder doesn’t necessarily mean the truck isn’t carrying hazardous materials, though. Federal regulations don’t require placards for every hazardous material or quantity.

When trucks do need placards, PHMSA requires them on both sides and both ends of the vehicle. Carriers must also keep the signs secure, readable, and visible. Federal regulations also prohibit misleading signs that resemble official hazmat placards. The rules specifically mention “Any sign, advertisement, slogan (such as ‘Drive Safely’), or device” that could be confused with an official warning placard.

A bare metal diamond, however, isn’t a hazard warning by itself. It’s simply a holder for the appropriate sign when the truck needs one.

U.S. Department of Transportation, Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration, “Identifying Hazardous Materials in Your Community” PHMSA, “DOT Chart 17: Markings, Labeling, and Placarding Guide” Labelmaster:, “Flip Placards” 49 CFR § 172.516, “Visibility and Display of Placards” 49 CFR § 172.502, “Prohibited and Permissive Placarding“

For instance, a compact inline driver may be easier to maneuver inside furniture, while a pistol-grip model can provide more power. Ahead, we explain what to look for and how the tested models compare so you can choose the best cordless screwdriver for your projects.

To earn a spot in our lineup, a cordless screwdriver had to be easy to use, durable, and capable of everyday fastening tasks, with a battery that lasted through small projects. We drove screws into drywall, pine, and birch, and tested the new models in prefab holes, predrilled holes, and raw wood to see where each performed best. The picks below offer useful options for projects around your home or workshop.

Right out of the box, the first thing we noticed about the Milwaukee M12 was its weight. At just over 2 pounds with the battery installed, it’s heavier than many cordless screwdrivers, but it fits nicely in the palm and isn’t too cumbersome for installing multiple screws. It made quick work of inserting screws in drywall, and we were able to insert screws in both pine and birch boards as well.

The M12 is less about fancy features and more about getting the job done. This pistol-grip screwdriver uses Milwaukee’s 12-volt lithium-ion batteries to create a mighty peak torque of 175 inch-pounds. It has an RPM range of up to 500, which makes setting fasteners quick work. The 2401-22 model uses a ¼-inch quick-change keyless chuck to swap out bits quickly, and it features a 15-position clutch to help regulate torque. We were also able to switch into drill mode to cancel the clutch feature.

Get the Milwaukee cordless screwdriver at The Home Depot or Ace Hardware.

As soon as we slipped the charged 12-volt battery into the Bosch PS21-2A cordless screwdriver and pulled the trigger, we could tell it offered more torque than most. It has two speed ranges we were able to switch between by sliding a lever on the top of the tool. The screwdriver generates up to 1,300 RPM at top speed, which is quite an accomplishment for an automatic screwdriver.

It also packs some powerful torque, which meant we were able to insert screws with ease into drywall, pine, and birch boards. With that much torque, the 21-adjustment clutch is essential to prevent stripping out the screw heads.

In addition to ample torque and speed, this screwdriver is compact, with a head length of just more than 5.5 inches. It comes with two 12-volt batteries and a charger. Plus, there’s a built-in LED light to help users see in dim locations, but it would be better if it were brighter. If DIYers want a cordless screwdriver to tackle some heavy-duty jobs, the Bosch PS21-2A ought to do the trick. It’s a powerful tool in a small package, weighing just 1.4 pounds.

Get the Bosch cordless screwdriver at Amazon or Lowe’s.

If your goal is to find a budget-friendly, light-duty cordless power screwdriver that won’t crush screws, the Black+Decker 4V MAX cordless screwdriver may fit the bill. We were impressed by its versatile features and even more impressed by its budget-friendly price. While this tool doesn’t generate as much torque as some picks in our lineup, it still drove drywall screws quickly. It wasn’t as successful with wood, but that’s not what this tool is intended to do.

This screwdriver has a three-position handle that swaps easily from a straight screwdriver to a 45-degree or right-angle driver in seconds. It uses ¼-inch driver bits, so users can swap between bits or employ the chuck as a ¼-inch nut driver.

The screwdriver boasts an unusually bright LED flashlight, making it easy to see in dark areas. The 4-volt, battery-operated screwdriver comes with two bits and a charger. Its 4-volt lithium-ion battery held a charge well throughout the testing, and this model features a built-in battery and a simple charger cord that plugs in directly.

Get the Black+Decker cordless screwdriver at Amazon, Lowe’s, or The Home Depot.

For all those little household fastener chores, such as installing outlet and switch plates, tightening cabinet or drawer screws, or hanging pictures on a wall, we think this lightweight Makita cordless screwdriver set is just the ticket. At just 3.6 volts, this cordless screwdriver is designed for light-duty applications, and it excels at that.

Instead of requiring the user to remove a battery, the DF001DW has an internal battery that charges via a USB cord plugged into a computer’s USB port or a standard outlet using the included AC adapter. We tested the DF001DW by inserting and removing screws in drywall and wood. It comes with an ample 81-piece accessory set boasting bits for most types of screw fasteners used today, including Phillips, flathead, and star bit. Plus, the tool has an LED guide light that can be turned on when desired (it doesn’t stay on automatically when the screwdriver is in use).

The DF001DW also converts from a pistol grip to a straight-barrel grip, making it even more versatile. It weighs less than a pound, so it didn’t slow us down—yet it offered ample power for inserting and removing screws, even in wood, without the tool’s motor bogging down.

Get the Makita 3.6V cordless screwdriver at Amazon.

The Kobalt is a compact screwdriver best suited to the small fastening jobs that crop up around the house. We tested it on dozens of screws, including fasteners for prefab holes, predrilled holes, and raw wood. At just 0.49 pounds, it was easy to maneuver while assembling furniture, and the soft-grip handle made it comfortable to hold through a string of screws.

Its 280-RPM motor runs at one speed, so there’s no trigger control for easing a screw into place. It also lacks an adjustable clutch to limit torque. We found it most useful for driving screws into prepared holes, where its 13.5 inch-pounds of maximum torque are better matched to the task. For screws going directly into raw wood, especially as resistance increased, we’d reach for a more powerful driver. The built-in LED helps illuminate the screw head, and the charge indicator lets us check the battery before starting a project.

The kit comes with a range of bits, a magnetic bit holder, a case, and a USB-C charging cable. That makes it convenient to keep together for furniture assembly and quick repairs.

Get the Kobalt cordless screwdriver at Lowe’s.

Having previously believed the power to an outlet was shut off only to suffer painful shocks, we know the value of being able to test an outlet in a pinch. So we were pretty impressed with the Skil cordless screwdriver’s ability to sense if the outlet was still hot, just by depressing a button on the top of the tool. The Skil emitted a sharp warning beep when we tested a hot outlet, and a red light flashed. When we tested a dead outlet, there was neither a light nor a beep. This built-in safety feature is a boon for those who don’t typically carry electrical testers around while doing DIY projects.

This compact cordless screwdriver boasts a dual-LED light, 10 changeable bits, and a micro USB charger. The chuck accepts any ¼-inch drive bit and also functions as a ¼-inch nut driver. It has both forward and reverse, but no adjustable clutch or speed settings. While it inserted screws effortlessly into drywall, it bogged down when driving screws into wood boards. Still, it’s so good at sensing circuits that you could reserve this cordless screwdriver solely for electrical maintenance jobs.

Get the Skil cordless screwdriver at Amazon, Menards, or Acme Tools.

The Amazon Basics (formerly Denali) screwdriver doesn’t boast many bells and whistles, but it lets you choose from three torque settings. We found that handy when inserting screws into materials with different densities—for instance, more torque when inserting screws in wood than in softer drywall. It also features an LED guide light, but we found it to be dim and unlikely to offer much illumination in low-light situations.

The screwdriver charges via a USB-C cord (included). We liked this setup, as it simplifies charging—no need to remove and charge the battery separately. A compact tool measuring about 7 inches long, it was useful in restricted spots, but we would have liked a convertible grip. A barrel grip is excellent in some situations, but a convertible pistol grip would add versatility.

The only real downside we noted was that this model tended to bog down a little when we inserted screws in wood. It did the job, but it took longer than it did on drywall. Still, this is a handy little cordless screwdriver to have around the house or to keep in the trunk of a car for when small jobs arise.

Get the Amazon Basics cordless screwdriver at Amazon.

We tested 12 cordless screwdrivers from 10 brands, considering price, battery design, included accessories, grip, speed, torque control, and features such as work lights and interchangeable heads. We drove dozens of fasteners with each tool, using prefab holes, predrilled holes, and raw wood; earlier tests also included drywall, pine, and birch.

We noted how comfortably each screwdriver fit in the hand, how easily we could change bits and direction, and whether the screwdriver had enough power to seat screws without damaging their heads. After testing, we rated each model on a five-point scale for ease of use, build quality, performance, and value, using those scores and our hands-on notes to select the picks in this guide.

A slim cordless screwdriver can reach spots a drill can’t as easily. A cordless screwdriver drives screws faster than a manual screwdriver and reduces wrist strain by eliminating the need for repeated wrist motions. Its light weight and battery power also make it easy to carry from one task to the next. As you shop, consider where you’ll use it and how much power and control your projects require.

The more power a cordless screwdriver has, the faster it can turn. While cordless screwdrivers don’t require the amount of power that a drill driver or an impact driver might have, they still need enough juice to get the job done. If you’re purchasing a straight barrel-type driver, consider one with a speed between 300 and 500 RPM. This range is ideal for loosening or tightening a screw quickly without being too fast to handle. With pistol-grip models, speeds above 1,000 RPM are easier to control.

The more torque your screwdriver has, the denser the material that it can drive a fastener into. Heavy-duty screwdrivers provide more torque and may be suitable for driving a few drywall screws into wood studs, but this can drain the battery quickly.

Small cordless screwdrivers can reach and manipulate various types of screws into awkward spaces much more easily than a manual tool can. As long as there’s room for the tip of the driver to fit onto the fastener, you’re set—a powered screwdriver will help do the rest.

To fit into such tight places, the best cordless screwdrivers are highly maneuverable. A slim, compact design helps, and many models also have rotating handles that swap from a straight grip to a pistol grip, like those seen on drills and screw guns. Also, a smaller battery size makes cordless screwdrivers easier to tuck between boards and other low-clearance scenarios, such as behind sinks for plumbing tasks.

Many cordless screwdrivers come with rechargeable batteries, and they tend to range between 4 and 8 volts. Since a cordless screwdriver requires much less speed and power than a drill, these lower voltages are adequate. Two benefits of a smaller, lower-voltage battery? It fits in smaller places than full-size options, and it helps make the rechargeable screwdriver as light as possible.

Some lower-end screwdrivers use replaceable batteries. These models are less convenient and more expensive, since you have to replace batteries frequently. They usually have less power and torque as well.

If you have a large project coming up, it helps if a cordless screwdriver has enough power to see it through to the end. Luckily, battery life isn’t much of a concern for most of the best cordless screwdrivers because their small motors don’t use as much battery energy as a large motor does.

However, some cordless screwdrivers have a battery-level indicator that alerts users when the battery is running low. It’s helpful to know the battery status so that you can juice it up while on a lunch or supply-run break. Many models take about an hour to recharge.

Cordless screwdrivers tighten or loosen screws in prethreaded holes. They’re perfect for screws in electrical boxes and fixtures, screws used in automotive interiors and appliances, installing door locks and cabinet hardware, and other mechanical settings with threaded holes.

Except for the most heavy-duty electrical screwdrivers, these tools aren’t typically designed for lag screws and bolts, wood screws, or fasteners in other dense materials. While it’s technically possible to drive a screw through drywall with one of these tools, that’s simply not the type of job they’re made for. For this situation, grab a drill or an impact driver instead.

Cordless screwdrivers use toolless chucks, so swapping between bits is quick and easy. These chucks fit ¼-inch bits—the same bits used in standard multi-bit manual screwdrivers. There are also ¼-inch-drive drill bits, allowing a screwdriver to be used as a drill in light-duty material like thin wood or plastics.

The variety of ¼-inch bits available makes cordless screwdrivers incredibly useful: For instance, you can alternate from driving Phillips head screws to removing Allen or Torx screws in seconds. Most cordless screwdrivers use magnets to hold the bits in place while also providing a bit of magnetism to keep the screw on the end of the bit.

The clutch in fastening tools regulates the amount of torque applied to a fastener. Once the set torque is reached, the clutch will start to “slip,” preventing the tool from driving the fastener or drilling any deeper. Simply adjust the clutch according to the fastener and material type. Since this is situation-specific, the rule of thumb is to set the clutch to a low setting and increase slowly as needed.

Too much torque can break smaller, older, or low-quality fasteners. Fortunately, the best cordless screwdrivers have adjustable clutch settings to avoid stripping or breaking these fasteners. The clutch can also avoid overdriving the screw too deeply, which may also cause unwanted results.

Torque settings can make a significant difference when working with old, stubborn fasteners. Instead of tearing the heads off screws or stripping the fastener beyond recognition, the clutch will begin to slip, preventing the driver from continuing to turn and causing damage.

Not all cordless screwdrivers have adjustable clutches, though. Some don’t have the power to require one. However, higher-end screwdrivers with more torque usually do.

By the time a project with a lot of assembly is finished, your forearm and hand might be tired from using a manual screwdriver. Lesson learned: To forgo hand and arm fatigue, opt for a cordless screwdriver. This’ll also save you energy and time, allowing you to move on to the next project faster.

Being able to see what you’re doing is key to a quality finished project. If, while using a drill, the tool keeps getting in the way, it may slip off the screw, marring the surface or scratching the workpiece. Cordless screwdrivers let users see what they’re doing since a hand won’t block the view.

Instead of carrying several screwdrivers around in a tool box or tool belt, it can be easier to tote just one cordless model. Since the bits are easy to swap, a complete bit set can reduce the overall weight and free up space in a belt for other tools. It’s much easier to carry one cordless screwdriver with eight tips than eight separate screwdrivers.

A cordless screwdriver is a tool that many reach for again and again for a host of different tasks. Here are a few ways to get the most help from this handy tool.

There’s a lot to consider when choosing a new cordless screwdriver, so you may still have questions. If you’re still wondering about the ins and outs of cordless screwdrivers, check out these answers to some commonly asked questions.

A cordless screwdriver is a battery-powered tool that tightens and loosens screws with a motor and trigger rather than relying on hand power.

Cordless drills for DIYers accept several drill bit sizes with adjustable chucks, while mini cordless screwdrivers only accept ¼-inch bits. Also, cordless drills tend to be more adjustable in terms of speed, letting the user drill into different materials accurately and efficiently.

There are a few slightly different methods for operating a cordless screwdriver, but here is a general usage guideline:1. Choose the right bit and place it in the chuck.2. Adjust the direction you want to drive the screw (tighten or loosen) with the switch on the screwdriver.3. Seat the bit completely into the head of the screw.4. Maintain pressure on the fastener and squeeze the trigger.

Yes, higher voltage tends to be better for cordless tools, but there are some caveats. Cordless tools with higher voltages are certainly more powerful, but that power comes at a cost. They weigh more and are less compact than lower-voltage options. For cordless screwdrivers, 4 to 8 volts is usually sufficient, especially for light-duty tasks.

Yes, but it depends on how often you’ll use them and the tasks you do most often. They can save quite a bit of time and effort and can increase your efficiency, all at a typically affordable price.

#7840. Lawprof's First Amendment Case Against Univ. of Kentucky, and a Case's "Journey so Circuitous it Would Make a Baggins Blush"

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Judge Benjamin Beaton Tuesday (W.D. Ky.) in Woodcock v. Capilouto (E.D. Ky.):

Ramsi Woodcock, a tenured University of Kentucky law professor, has been under investigation for more than a year for controversial comments regarding Israel and Palestine. The alleged comments varied in both content and forum: an online petition calling for the invasion of Israel, listserv blasts to the University faculty and broader legal academy accusing Israel of genocide, the interjection of far-afield remarks about colonization at an antitrust panel in Hong Kong, shouts of "Free Palestine!" while driving two law students near campus, and more.

None of the remarks came in the classroom and none appears to have disrupted school activities. Yet all related in some manner to his role as a state-employed professor—rendering all the more curious the University's July 2025 decisions to promote him to full professor one week and call him in for questioning (literally) the next. {Curiouser still, Woodcock maintains that the remarks in question dated as far back as February 2024 and were known (at least in part) to the University since March 2024.}

The following week brought a public denunciation from the University's President, the start of a formal investigation into potential harassment under Title VI, reassignment from teaching duties to "professional development," and a (since rescinded) ban from campus. {This first of two "Notice[s] of Investigation" laid out four allegations that Woodcock "may have violated" the University's code of conduct and other policies. The notice declared (without elaboration) that the "investigation … is consistent with the First Amendment" and "addresses requirements under Title VI of the Civil Rights Act." A second notice, based on reports from four students, identified four additional allegations that may have "created a hostile environment on the basis of race, color, or national origin."}

Rather than participate in the investigation, however, Woodcock filed this [federal] lawsuit …. The pleadings characterize his treatment by leaders of the University and its law school as retaliation for protected academic or personal speech, violations of the Due Process and Establishment Clauses, and racial and religious discrimination…. The issue ripe for resolution today is Woodcock's request for temporary emergency relief halting the investigation and reinstating his teaching duties.

This is Woodcock's second or third such request, depending on how one counts. And it follows a journey so circuitous it would make a Baggins blush.

The judge previously assigned to this case held a preliminary-injunction hearing in December 2025. Instead of granting or denying interim equitable relief, however, that judge decided to abstain [under Younger v. Harris] on the ground that the University investigation should precede any federal adjudication. The Sixth Circuit, in the spring and summer of 2026, declined to issue a stay, reversed on appeal, and declined to accelerate the mandate. {See Woodcock v. University of Kentucky (6th Cir. 2026) (Because the "the disciplinary proceedings against Woodcock remain[ed] in a preliminary, investigatory stage," the proceedings were not "ongoing," rendering Younger abstention inapplicable). Concurring with the denial of Woodcock's request to immediately issue the mandate, Judge Gilman wrote that "the panel's opinion" did not "in any way limi[t] the sound discretion of the district court regarding how to proceed on remand," but instead "simply h[eld] that the district court erred in declining to accept jurisdiction based on Younger" without "purport[ing] to dictate what should happen upon remand; i.e., whether the district court should immediately proceed with a ruling on Woodcock's preliminary-injunction motion, or whether it should first consider the University's motion to dismiss, or whether it should stay proceedings to allow for the University to complete its investigation."}

Woodcock, meanwhile, filed a parallel lawsuit and TRO request in state court in September 2026—relief that the Franklin (County) Circuit Judge denied without prejudice. {The Franklin Circuit Court consolidated the new case's request [for] a TRO with the First Amendment suit Woodcock originally filed in federal court seeking to prevent former-Judge Van Tatenhove from assuming his role as dean of the UK Law School. After this Court denied his requests for emergency relief, Woodcock voluntarily dismissed the federal claims and refiled in state court.} The Sixth Circuit then remanded and reassigned this federal case to a judge outside the Eastern District after one of that court's [judges] was appointed dean of the law school. Woodcock had previously filed still another lawsuit—also reassigned here, and also to eventually land in state court—seeking to block the dean's appointment on First Amendment grounds. The University investigation (led by a private law firm) resumed in September. And this Court held a TRO hearing in October. Although the investigator anticipated that this phase of the investigation would finish by November 2, that date has come and gone.

Such unusual litigation can raise unusual—and unusually tricky—legal questions. This is true here, even though the crux of Woodcock's claim is superficially simple: the University leaders (Defendants here) took adverse action (investigation and reassignment) against him because of his constitutionally protected speech (chiefly, at least on his telling, Woodcock's self-titled "Petition for Military Action Against Israel"). But resolving this question, at least in the context of preliminary equitable relief, raises several others that Supreme Court precedent leaves significantly undertheorized.

None of the answers to these questions are obvious based on the record in this Court or the precedential decisions of others. Whether an investigation into speech and related conduct amounts to unconstitutional retaliation depends on whether the First Amendment protected the underlying speech and whether the state's response would deter a person of "ordinary firmness" from speaking similarly. Protection for the speech, in turn, depends on whether Woodcock spoke in either his personal or his "academic" capacity. And even if one of those carve-outs apply, courts may still ask whether the "employee's interest in speaking on a matter of public concern outweigh[s] the employer's interest 'in promoting the efficiency of the public services it performs through its employees.'" {Courts also consider "whether the statement (a) impairs discipline by superiors or harmony among co-workers, (b) has a detrimental impact on close working relationships for which personal loyalty and confidence are necessary, (c) impedes the performance of the speaker's duties or interferes with the regular operation of the enterprise," or (d) undermines the mission of the employer."} Additionally, the appropriateness of interim equitable relief turns on similarly difficult—even incommensurable—considerations, including the burdens on Woodcock's ongoing political speech (which appears to have continued in forums outside the classroom), the Commonwealth's interest in controlling the taxpayer-subsidized education offered to its citizens and future officers of the court, and the public's interest in open dialogue, effective investigations, and the avoidance of harassment.

Each of these determinations, courts have illustrated time and again, is fact-dependent. And although a previous judge held an evidentiary hearing nearly a year ago, time and events have not stood still. Woodcock has not, at least not yet, shown that the mere fact of an investigation would chill an ordinary speaker (to say nothing of a tenured professor) in these strange circumstances from engaging in speech on public questions inside or outside the classroom. After all, a university has an interest in "determin[ing] for itself on academic grounds who may teach, what may be taught, how it shall be taught, and who may be admitted to study."

Nor has Woodcock yet shown that the idiosyncratic lawprof speech at issue—in listservs, foreign conferences, links from the UK website, carpools, and the like—is necessarily protected, heedless of forum or audience. {For instance, whether institutional IT policies that restrict a professor's use of school email resources amounts to a "prior restraint," is hardly clear given the prevalence of content-neutral time/place/manner restrictions. And whether a professor's off-topic panel remarks amount to an unprotected "shout-down" or instead protected academic speech, for example, likewise casts at least some doubt on Woodcock's argument that this amounts to pure academic or political speech.} To be sure, whether he spoke in his professorial capacity is hotly contested by the parties—and cannot be determined with confidence or specificity at this stage.

Whether reassignment from all teaching duties would deter a speaker in a retaliatory manner is a closer question. This is particularly true because the University has seemingly identified no past or future campus disruption, little risk that Woodcock's speech has or will infect classroom instruction, and any reason why responses other than prior restraint would be unavailable if Woodcock stepped outside the bounds of his role in the future. On the other hand, Woodcock hasn't convincingly identified any aspect of this investigation or reassignment that is vindictive, disproportionately burdensome, or otherwise out of the ordinary.

Such showings are neither obvious nor obviously foreclosed on the current record. Indeed, they are not susceptible to prudent resolution by a distant district judge in the middle of a semester, when interim relief measured in two- or four-week increments [the duration of typical TROs -EV] is highly unlikely to benefit Woodcock in a manner that outweighs the concomitant disruption to the University's orderly governance of academic affairs. Since Woodcock bears the burden of justifying temporary emergency relief, but has not carried it, the Court must deny his TRO request. When in doubt, the Sixth Circuit has reminded us, "[t]he administration of the university rests not with the courts, but with the administrators of the institution.

These are important questions worthy of further evidentiary presentation, however. To that end, the Court will schedule a second preliminary-injunction hearing later this month. The balance between state governance and individual speech can tilt too far in either direction, of course, and investigations cannot last forever. In hopes of limiting any federal judicial intervention to its appropriate role, and with "reluctan[ce] to trench on the prerogatives of state and local educational institutions," therefore, the Court sets a preliminary-injunction hearing for Thursday, November 19 ….

UPDATE: I originally stated that the case was from the Western District of Kentucky, and the opinion does indeed have that heading. But, as the text of the opinion explains, the case is being litigated in the Eastern District of Kentucky, though Judge Beaton is a judge of the Western District (who is, for this particular case, sitting by designation in the Eastern District).

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

#7839. We Tested Ryobi’s $129 Pressure Washer — Here’s What It Can (and Can’t) Do

Can this portable power washer possibly compare to the real thing? We put it to the test.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Nothing sets you up for a better spring than taking some time for some seasonal cleaning in the fall, and one of the best tools for autumn home cleanup is a classic pressure washer. If you’ve got a surface or a screen you need sprayed, a pressure washer can deliver enough pressure for all kinds of scrubbing.

But even the most avid pressure washer advocates would tell you they’re also pretty cumbersome tools that require a lot of setup and garage storage space. That’s exactly why I wanted to try out this portable pressurized washer from Ryobi. The concept is intriguing, promising users a fraction of the size, cost and power of a standard pressure washer. I was very curious whether this tool would actually provide more cleaning power than a standard garden hose nozzle.

The first thing I noticed when unboxing the Ryobi One Plus Electric Power Cleaner was how substantial the tool felt. I was expecting it to feel a little flimsy, but the tool felt well-built in my hands. It all assembled easily in just a few clicks, taking only a small fraction of the time it would’ve taken to set up a full-size pressure washer. And if you’re worried about water ruining your battery, don’t be. The entire battery chamber is enclosed by a tightly sealed plastic housing.

For this test, I decided to replicate a classic fall cleanup task: hosing down screens. I wanted a big surface to clean, so I pulled the screen door off the back door and set it up in the backyard. Then, I applied a light coating of flour to the middle of the screen and a light mist of water to lock the flour in place.

From there, I just had to finish setting up the Ryobi pressure washer. It comes with three different nozzles: two flat angled nozzles and one “turbo nozzle” that sprays the water in a speedy spiral. All I had to do was attach the pressure washer to a garden hose, and the tool was ready to go. Then I just set myself up in front of the screen with the pressure washer the recommended distance (1-2 feet) from the screen. ‘

All that was left to do was let it rip. The first thing that stands out when you use this portable pressure washer is that it feels a little underwhelming when you pull the trigger- especially if you’ve ever used a full-sized pressure washer. There’s not much kick, and the water leaves the nozzle at a steady but uninspiring speed. For a few seconds, I was worried the 700psi of pressure wouldn’t be enough to clean up the floury mess I’d created.

But my worries lessened the longer I used the tool. It was gentler than the pressure washers I’d used before, but it provided a consistent stream that quickly started knocking the flour loose from the screen. Things started going even better once I switched to the turbo nozzle. The spin action really helped compensate for the lack of PSI pressure. Within another minute, I had knocked off a ton of the sticky flour from the screen.

A post shared by Family Handyman (@familyhandyman)

So enough waffling… what’s the verdict? It’s pretty clear, as soon as you start using this tool, that the Ryobi tool isn’t going to fully replace a full-sized pressure washer… especially if you need to really blast something. But there are many use cases for a pressure washer where consistency is more important than power. And if you’ve ever accidentally damaged something with a pressure washer, the reduced power of this tool might even be something you consider a pro.

It took a while, but eventually the screen was sparkling clean- so clean, in fact, it was nearly invisible in the doorway. I should also point out that real-world conditions are rarely as messy as the sticky flour mess I created. If you just need to get dust off a screen or mud off a sidewalk, this tool is a significant upgrade over a simple stream from a garden hose. Ultimately, you’re trading power for portability, and whether that works for you will depend on the job you have to tackle. If it’s only needed for routine seasonal cleaning, this pressure washer could be perfect for you.

Just don’t expect it to peel paint off a pole.

#7838. What Does a Green Porch Light Mean? The Tradition, Explained
